title: Dairy calf and heifer rearing, feeding and health care

lessons.title: The newborn calf and colostrum
lessons.html:
The future herd starts at birth

Every heifer calf is a future milk cow. Poor rearing leads to deaths, slow growth, late first calving and lower lifetime yield. As a supervisor you set and enforce the calf protocol.

At calving

  • Calve cows in a clean, dry, sheltered camp or pen, not in muddy yards.
  • Check the calf is breathing; clear mucus from the nose and mouth.
  • Dip or spray the navel with an antiseptic as the farm protocol and vet advise, to prevent navel infections.
  • Identify the calf with ear tags and record dam, date, sex and any assistance needed at birth.

Colostrum: the most important feed

Calves are born without protective antibodies. They get them only from colostrum, the first milk. The calf's gut can absorb antibodies well only for a short time after birth, and this ability falls quickly over the first day. Rules:

  1. Feed colostrum as soon as possible after birth, ideally within the first few hours.
  2. Feed enough: the volume should follow your farm's protocol as set with the vet, often based on the calf's body weight.
  3. Use good-quality colostrum; test it with a colostrometer or Brix refractometer if the farm does.
  4. Feed with a bottle or, if the calf will not drink, by oesophageal tube, used only by trained staff.
  5. Store surplus good colostrum frozen and thaw gently in warm water, never by boiling or microwaving at high power.

Hygiene

Collect colostrum in clean buckets, feed from clean bottles and teats, and wash all equipment after every feed. Dirty equipment introduces the bacteria that cause calf scours.

Housing

Calves do well in individual hutches or pens that are dry, draught-free but well ventilated, with clean bedding. Separate calves from the adult herd to reduce disease spread.

lessons.title: Feeding and growing calves and heifers
lessons.html:
Milk feeding phase

Calves are fed whole milk or milk replacer, usually twice a day, at consistent times, temperatures and concentrations. Mix milk replacer exactly to the manufacturer's instructions; wrong mixing causes scours.

  • Offer clean, fresh water from the first week.
  • Offer calf starter (a palatable concentrate) early; it develops the rumen.
  • Introduce good-quality roughage as advised by the nutritionist.

Weaning

Wean when calves eat enough starter consistently, rather than only by age. Reduce milk gradually to avoid a growth check. Weigh or measure calves to monitor growth.

Heifer rearing

After weaning, heifers need balanced feeding to grow steadily to target weights for first insemination and calving. Underfed heifers calve late; overfat heifers may have calving difficulties and lower milk production. Group heifers by size to reduce bullying at the feed trough.

Health care

ProblemSignsPrevention
Scours (diarrhoea)Loose faeces, dehydration, sunken eyesColostrum, hygiene, consistent milk feeding
PneumoniaCoughing, fast breathing, nasal discharge, feverVentilation without draughts, dry bedding
Navel illSwollen, hot, painful navelNavel dipping, clean calving area
Tick-borne diseasesFever, weakness, anaemiaTick control as the vet advises

Treat scouring calves early with oral electrolytes as your protocol directs, and keep feeding milk unless the vet says otherwise. Call the vet for calves that are down, cold or not drinking.

Vaccination and controlled diseases

Follow the farm's vaccination programme drawn up with the vet. Brucellosis vaccination of heifer calves is a legal requirement under animal disease control rules in South Africa; the vet will advise on timing and approved vaccines. Record every vaccination and treatment with product, dose, date and withdrawal period.

Key points

  • Colostrum soon after birth is critical for calf immunity.
  • Clean equipment and dry housing prevent scours and pneumonia.
  • Offer water and starter early; wean on intake, not just age.
  • Grow heifers steadily to target weights for first calving.
  • Follow the vet's vaccination plan, including brucellosis for heifers, and record all treatments.
